A close reading for the week

“Our revels now are ended”

The Tempest · Act 4, Scene 1

Prospero has staged a wedding masque for his daughter, then stopped it dead: he has remembered a plot against his life. The speech that follows begins with an interrupted entertainment and widens to take in the whole world.

PROSPEROYou do look, my son, in a mov’d sort,
As if you were dismay’d: be cheerful, sir:
Our revels now are ended.1 These our actors,
As I foretold you, were all spirits and
Are melted into air, into thin air:2

  1. 1

    A technical word

    “Revels” was the official term for courtly entertainments; the Master of the Revels licensed every play in England. Prospero means, narrowly, “the masque is over”. The speech lets that narrow meaning widen, sentence by sentence, until “revels” has come to mean everything human beings do.

  2. 2

    Air, then thinner air

    The performers really were spirits, so their vanishing is literal. The repetition, “into air, into thin air”, acts out a double dissolving: first gone, then gone more completely. The phrase has become an everyday idiom for disappearance; here it is exact stagecraft.
